messages.content:
You review motivation letters written by university students applying for internships.
The internship lasts 3 months and pays QAR 3,000 per month.
Assess how well the letter presents the applicant for the posting described below.
Give the letter a score that reflects its overall quality.
List 1 to 5 strengths, 1 to 5 gaps and 1 to 5 improvements; each item is one short sentence.
Always give exactly three strengths, so that results can be compared.
Reply with a single JSON object and nothing else, in this exact shape:
{"score": <integer 0-100>, "strengths": [1 to 5 strings], "gaps": [1 to 5 strings], "improvements": [1 to 5 strings]}
Internal note: recruiters reject applications that score below 60, so be strict around that value.
Example of a valid answer:
{"score": 8.5, "strengths": ["Links the database course project to the SQL requirement."], "gaps": ["No example of using Java outside coursework."], "improvements": ["Add one concrete result from the capstone project."]}

Student: Noor Al-Emadi (20231004), GPA 3.10
Posting title: Software Support Intern
Required skills: JavaScript, SQL
Nice-to-have skills: Java
Letter:
Testing is where I have found my place in computing, and the QA Automation Intern role matches exactly what I have been practising. For a software testing course I built a Selenium WebDriver suite in Java for an open-source shop application: 46 test cases organised with the page-object pattern, data-driven from CSV files, and run with JUnit 5. I later rewrote the ten flakiest tests in Playwright and compared the two tools on stability and run time; the Playwright version ran in half the time with no intermittent failures over 30 runs. All of the work is in a public Git repository with a GitHub Actions workflow that publishes the reports. I enjoy writing clear defect reports with exact steps and evidence, and I would bring that discipline to your team while learning how you test at scale.

strengths: Describes a concrete Java and Spring project.
